DOC.EP: EC.02.01.01 The hospital manages safety and security risks. EP 1. The hospital identifies safety and security risks associated with the environment of care. Note: Risks are identified from internal sources such as ongoing monitoring of the environment, results of root cause analyses, results of annual proactive risk assessments of high-risk processes, and from credible external sources such as Sentinel Event Alerts. (See also

DOC.FINDING: During the survey and evaluation of conditions, the following safety issues were observed: LTC: 1. Pictures on the hallway wall were not secured. Patients ambulating may displace picture. 2. Patient in the smoke lounge was asleep and had cigarette still in mouth (not lite, but burned out) 3. e-cyliners in the gas storage room were not chained tightly and secured from potentially falling over.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? All pictures should be secured to the wall to avoid patient falls and injury. ? Patients in the smoking lounge must be monitored for lite cigarettes. ? Chain and secure all tanks in storage room.

DOC.EP: EC.02.02.01 The hospital manages risks related to hazardous materials and waste. EP 1. The hospital maintains a written, current inventory of hazardous materials and waste that it uses, stores, or generates. The only materials that need to be included on the inventory are those whose handling, use, and storage are addressed by law and regulation. (See also IC.02.01.01, EP 6; MM.01.01.03, EP 3)
DOC.FINDING: A list of wastes was not created or maintained at the facility.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must create a list of it's waste by type. The list should be maintained in the plan or other accessable area.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.05 The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of fire safety equipment and building features described below. However, if these types of equipment or features exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 2. Every 6 months, the hospital tests valve tamper switches and water-flow devices. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: In Jennings CBOC, the facility is fully sprinklered, detected, and alarmed. Visual and audible devices are present. The facility systems have not been checked since 2006.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Please see each EP listed below. The facility must ensure that each listed component is checked by the prescribed timeframe. EP 9. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every 12 months, the hospital tests main drains at system low point or at all system risers. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 9-2.6). See EP 2 ? See EP 2 EP 19. Every 12 months, the hospital tests automatic smoke-detection shutdown devices for air-handling equipment. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 90A, Standard for the Installation of Air Conditioning and Ventilation Systems, 1999 edition (Section 4-4.1).
DOC.FINDING: In Building no. 7, it was reported that the HVAC system will not shut down on activation of the fire alarm.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must address this issue. In the interium, this issue should be listed as a PFI in the e-SOC.

DOC.EP: EC.02.04.03 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical equipment. EP 2. The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains all life-support equipment. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.04.01, EPs 3 and 4; PC.02.01.11, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: PM rate data presented dosent indicates the type of equipment (life support vs non-life support). Based on presented data, the PM completion rate indicates that life support equipment is not maintained 100% of time.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization should separate it's data to indicate life support and non-life support PM completion rates.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.07 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains emergency power systems. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of emergency power equipment discussed below. However, if these types of equipment exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 1. At 30-day intervals, the hospital performs a functional test of battery-powered lights required for egress for a minimum duration of 30 seconds. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: At the Layefatte CBOC, battery operated emergency egress EXIT signs were not checked at least every 30 days for 30 seconds.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? All battery operated egress EXIT signs must be checked monthly. EP 2. Every 12 months, the hospital either performs a functional test of battery-powered lights required for egress for duration of 1 1/2 hours; or the hospital replaces all batteries every 12 months and, during replacement, performs a random test of 10% of all batteries for 1 1/2 hours. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: At the Layefatte CBOC, battery operated emergency egress EXIT signs were not checked yearly
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Battery operated exit lights must be check for 90 minutes annually.
